verdicts.trueWording: basic math screwed up; no complication inflicted after the success
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched live (200, browser UA), dated December 28th, 2025. Both named violations are on the page in the Lasers & Feelings playtest: at character creation ChatGPT "almost immediately screws up basic math" ("Number: 3 (balanced but slightly leaning Lasers)" - 3 leans Feelings), it mis-states the target number ("Under 3 counts as a success" - "This is incorrect. A 3 would also count as a success"), and after the first successful roll "The GM did not inflict a complication, harm, or cost." Claim carries no quote field, so substance grade. Precision point: the article's own "two mechanics" of this one-page game are the action roll and Helping; both errors the claim names are action-roll rules (Helping is never shown violated), so "two core mechanics" reads correctly only as the two rules the parenthetical enumerates.

verdicts.trueWording: "You're telling people things. You want to SHOW people things."
verdicts.note: Quote appears word for word (curly apostrophe in original). Both read-aloud specimens are on the page verbatim: "Suddenly, in the distance, you hear the desperate cry of a woman in distress!" and "a black skull mask to his face, a cursed artifact that emanates a palpable malevolence". The "instead of letting players feel it" limb is the next sentence: "We want them to feel it, visceral. Not be told it."

verdicts.trueWording: "the prose reeks of either EASL or AI"; "write a response in ChatGPT Style"
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim (Anonymous, June 1 2024). Plural "commenters" is right: Lonely Penguin "Pretty clearly written by AI" and Yomar "clearly written using an LLM" as well. The publisher (1st Adventures team) posted a reply June 2, and Anonymous answered "Motherfuckers even write a response in ChatGPT Style. Oof.", with another commenter reproducing a ChatGPT-generated version of that reply. Hooks limb verbatim in Bryce's text: "The standard please help me stuff, very abstract, in about one sentence."

verdicts.trueWording: "Note the padding. Note how it doesn't say ANYTHING."
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. The opener is on the page exactly as claimed ("Arriving at the house, the PCs see a strange sight: the structure appears to be ..." - "This then is the opening line of the first real room"), as is the deletability limb: "You can literally delete everything here and not impact the adventure in any way at all." The "every encounter" limb is the page's "And encounter after encounter does this, is like this" plus "This is the normal manner for this adventure" - repetition-across-encounters, phrased as recurrence rather than a literal universal.

verdicts.trueWording: "A tell-tale sign of ChatGPT, btw. It's its default style"
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim from commenter Max Z (Nov 25 2024), continuing "...if you ask it to 'write a room description for a D&D game'". Both remaining limbs verbatim in the same comment: "you can tell it to 'be brief' and it cuts this shit out without any problem" and "But the author would have to understand that this padding is meaningless first".

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "Commenters" (plural) - exactly one comment on the page makes this point (Anonymous, Nov 26 2024, 1:04 am); no second commenter says it
verdicts.trueWording: One commenter laments the mediocre D&D corpus ChatGPT trained on
verdicts.note: Quote is on the page word for word, inside the whole comment: "If only the typical D&D adventure writing ChatGPT was trained on was good". The substance - style inheriting the mediocrity of the training corpus - is carried by that single wry conditional; it is the entire comment, with no elaboration. Downgraded on the plural attribution only, which matters because this chunk's neighbouring claims (391) genuinely do rest on several commenters.

verdicts.trueWording: be more specific than "wicked": wiry fur, fangs, red eyes
verdicts.note: No quote field, so substance grade. The contrast is explicit in Bryce's review of the bird/goat: "I might be more specific than 'wicked' in a description ... wiry brustle fur, sharp fangs and blood red eyes or some such" (page's own typo "brustle"), set against the module's "small, wicked-looking six-legged three-eyed winged goat". So: weak abstract adjective named, concrete alternative supplied.

verdicts.trueWording: "it's full of second person narrative, YOU step off the boat. YOU see a so and so."
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in Bryce's text. The intro-read-aloud limb is supported: "The long read-aloud literally has you stepping off your boat on to the dock and seeing a sign on the tavern door", "a page of single column read-aloud ... all on monologue form". Attribution limb verbatim from commenter Max Z (June 13 2024): "I bet that's also where the abundance of second person comes too - ChatGPT does it by default unless you tell it 'not to describe my actions'."

verdicts.trueWording: "a year ago ... this is the _exact_ phrase the AI was giving me for some corridor"
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, ending Max Z's comment: "Basically, if the prompts are all the same, the results will be almost or exactly the same." Every limb holds: "a year ago", a different adventure ("one of OSRIC sewers adventures (AA25, Beneath the Heart of Empire)"), and the exact corridor phrase - he quotes back the module's "The air is thick with the stench of decay..." line. "Same prompt, same output" is his stated principle rather than a claim that his prompt was byte-identical.

verdicts.trueWording: "There's no real distinction between when read-aloud starts and when it stops. It just sort of all runs together"
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Typographic limb is explicit: the adventure "IMMEDIATELY shifts to DM text, with no change in font, or shading, or section heading" (also "one paragraph break suddenly turns in to DM text again"). Attention limb verbatim: "the intro read-aloud text being Looooong, diverting players focus from paying attention."

verdicts.trueWording: stench of decay, dripping water echoes off damp walls
verdicts.note: No quote field, so substance grade - though the fragment embedded in the claim matches the page word for word. The line is the module's sewer-descent opener, quoted by Bryce and then quoted back by commenter Max Z, who says ChatGPT gave him "the _exact_ phrase" a year earlier - that is what makes it "the predictable generated sensory opener". Dock limb verbatim: encounters one to three on the docks share "some read-aloud that is to be used for all three of these encounters" / "used for all three of the encounters, exactly the same".

verdicts.trueWording: EVERYTHING gets a backstory; read-aloud over-reveals; commenter asks about AI
verdicts.note: No quote field, so substance grade; all three limbs are nonetheless verbatim on the page. Backstory: "The fucking adventure is FULL of backstory. EVERYTHING gets a backstory." Read-aloud: "the read-aloud text also over-reveals information. Why engage in the trivial back and forth between the DM and players that is the heart of the game when you can now get all of the details in the read-aloud" (Bryce's sarcasm, i.e. players need not engage). Commenter Philipp (Aug 8 2024): "I had the feeling this publisher relies heavily on AI, both text and illustrations. Would you say is this apparent in this module?"

verdicts.trueWording: "just generating plausible word-sequences and has no idea what it means"
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in Hemlock's commentary (Dec 21 2022) on an F# answer relayed from Reddit: "ChatGPT's 'explanation' is superficially plausible as technobabble, but deeply untrustworthy in the same way as Star Trek technobabble." The inspection limb is his next clause: "unlike a good explanation, it doesn't become more clear as you study it more closely ... instead it becomes more clear that chatGPT is just generating plausible word-sequences" - i.e. scrutiny exposes the emptiness rather than clarifying the explanation, which the claim renders as getting less clear on inspection.

verdicts.trueWording: "the Bot does not understand the implications of 'up' and 'down'"
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim (Beoric, Dec 19 2022): "it thought it was reasonable that you could fall through trap doors on the ceiling." The generated text is on the same page twice, in two separate bot outputs: "The ceiling of this room is dotted with numerous trap doors ... Any character standing beneath one of these trap doors when it is triggered will fall through, taking 1d6 points of damage", and the regenerated trick room's "The ceiling is dotted with trap doors that open and close at random intervals, forcing the characters to duck and weave to avoid falling through." Plural "rooms" therefore holds.

verdicts.trueWording: "The 'burst of flame' has no damage stats though; it's pure fluff with no effect"
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim (Hemlock, Dec 19 2022), posted in direct reply to Maynard's quoted line "Interesting to see that even AI can write a better kitchen than most of the dreck Bryce reads." The "generated" limb was confirmed by also fetching page 3 of the same thread, where Beoric's ChatGPT output reads: "There is a trap in the room that will release a burst of flames if triggered, which has a one in six chance of affecting any creatures in the room" - no damage dice anywhere in it. Only the generating text itself sits on page 3; the assessment quoted is on page 4.
